n: God now describes Leviathan, a terrifying sea creature. It may be a crocodile pictured larger than life, and it also symbolizes the forces of chaos that only God can master. Can Job catch it with a fishhook?

f.g: A great sea monster — possibly the crocodile, and in poetry a symbol of chaos and evil.

n: Can Job put a rope through its nose or pierce its jaw with a hook, as people did with captured fish or prisoners?

f.w: bore his jaw through with a thorn
f.g: Fish were sometimes kept on a hook or ring through the jaw.

n: Will Leviathan beg Job for mercy or speak to him gently?
Will it make a covenant to be Job’s servant forever?
Can Job play with it like a pet bird or put it on a leash for his young daughters?

f.g: Leash him as a pet for girls.

n: Will traders bargain over it or divide it among merchants like a catch of fish?

f.g: Literally “Canaanites,” who were known as traders.

n: Can Job fill its hide with harpoons or its head with fishing spears?
Just lay a hand on it once — you will remember the fight and never try again!

f.w: remember the battle, do no more

n: Any hope of capturing it is false; just seeing it knocks a person flat.

f.w: cast down even at the sight of him
f.g: Overwhelmed by fear just by looking.

n: No one is fierce enough to provoke it. Then who could stand against God, who made it? This is the heart of the speech.

f.w: who then is able to stand before me?

n: Who has given God anything first, so that God owes him? Everything under heaven belongs to God.

f.w: whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine

n: God will not keep silent about Leviathan’s limbs, its great strength, and its graceful form.
Who can strip off its outer armor or approach it with a double bridle?

f.g: Its outer coat — its scaly hide.

n: Who would dare open its jaws, ringed with terrifying teeth?
Its back has rows of shields, sealed tightly together. (A crocodile’s back is covered with bony plates.)

f.g: Possibly “his back is rows of shields.”

n: The scales lie so close that no air can get between them.

f.w: no air can come between them

n: They are welded together and cannot be pried apart.
Its sneezes flash with light, and its eyes glow like the rays of dawn.
Flames shoot from its mouth and sparks fly out — poetic language that makes Leviathan a dragon-like symbol of overwhelming power.
Smoke pours from its nostrils like steam from a boiling pot over burning reeds.
Its breath sets coals on fire, and a flame comes from its mouth.
Strength lives in its neck, and terror dances ahead of it.

f.w: sorrow is turned into joy before him

n: The folds of its flesh are tightly joined and immovable.
Its heart is as hard as rock, hard as a lower millstone.

f.g: The lower millstone, which was especially hard to withstand constant grinding.

n: When it rises, even the mighty are terrified and lose control in panic.

f.w: by reason of breakings they purify themselves
f.g: Better “they are beside themselves with fear.”

n: Sword, spear, dart, or javelin — none can harm it.

f.g: Here probably a javelin (elsewhere, a coat of mail).

n: It treats iron like straw and bronze like rotten wood.
Arrows don’t make it run, and slingstones are like chaff to it.
Clubs are like straw, and it laughs at the rattle of a javelin.

f.w: he laugheth at the shaking of a spear

n: Its underside is like jagged pottery, leaving marks in the mud like a threshing sledge.

f.g: A threshing sledge — a board studded with stones.

n: It makes the deep churn like a boiling pot and the sea like a pot of mixing perfume.

f.g: A jar of perfume being stirred.

n: It leaves a glittering wake behind it; one would think the deep had white hair.
Nothing on earth equals it — a creature made without fear.

f.w: Upon earth there is not his like

n: It looks down on all the proud; it is king over every proud beast. Only God is above it — and Job is invited to trust the God who rules even this.

f.w: a king over all the children of pride
